title: One vocabulary for the whole app
why: The same thing has up to eight names across modules — the attention list, approvals, money still owed, tickets, members, stages, trades — so a studio owner can't trust that two screens mean the same thing.
rule: Adopt one glossary and use it everywhere: Needs your attention (was Needs you · To do · Needs my review…) · Approvals (was To approve · Needs your OK · Your OK) · Payments for a project's money tab (was Money), with Client payments and Costs inside it and in Finance (was Money in · Money out · Billing) · To collect / To pay / Collected / Paid for money · Issues (was Tickets · Escalations) · Members (never Team · People · Collaborators) · Client (never Homeowner) · Trade (never Category) · Stage only for a lead's or a project's stage. The Words table lists every change.

title: One verb on a row — the rest in its ⋮
why: Rows repeat three to five purple text actions (Members has 28 on one screen, Tasks 63), so the eye can't find the one thing a row is for.
rule: Every list row shows at most one action — the DS secondary text button — and everything else moves into the row's ⋮ (PortalMenu). No 'Open' beside a ⋮: the row itself opens. Hover tools never cover a row's own cells.

title: One filled button per screen
why: Several screens carry two to four filled buttons (the lead page, the project's Money tab, Integrations, the Visualizer editor), and some offer a move the page will refuse.
rule: A screen has at most one filled button, for its one job; it is never a state ('Shared with client') and never a move the page knows it will refuse. Everything else is outlined or text.

title: Say each thing once
why: The same fact or next step is printed three to five times on one page (a project's next step, a lead's dates, X-Ray's difference, a held meeting's concerns).
rule: One fact lives in one place on a screen: the header's next step is not repeated in a card, a banner and a row; a tag never repeats the heading or the status pill next to it.

title: Explanations off the page
why: Paragraphs and 'how it works' boxes sit on every visit (Members' five lines, every Settings module's signposts, 3,000–5,000 px help-heavy pages, prototype disclaimers on studio screens).
rule: A screen says what it is in one line. Longer help goes behind a 'How this works' link or the house Tooltip, and a tool's how-it-works shows on the first visit only. Prototype / demo talk never sits on a studio's screen.

title: Capitals only for a status
why: CAPITAL tags carry dates, counts, names, topics and property types ('29 SEP ’26', 'HDB 4-ROOM', 'MANDATORY' on 34 of 38 rows), so a real status no longer stands out.
rule: Uppercase is kept for status tags only (Draft, Sent, Overdue …). Meta (a date, a type, a count, a name) is sentence-case secondary text; card heads are one style — bold sentence case.

title: Counts only where they help — one way to write them
why: Numbers sit on every chip and tab (Marketplace shows 11 on its first screen), are written five ways ('Needs you 51', 'Overdue · 6', '(48)', 'Open (3)', '4 to approve'), and the rail wears six red badges at rest.
rule: A count shows only where it changes a decision (what waits on you); it is written one way ('Label · n'); a red badge means overdue-and-yours only, everything else is a quiet count or nothing.

title: Empty means quiet
why: Columns of '--', 'Not set', 'No preferences set', 'Nothing yet' run down lists and info columns, written three ways ('--', '- -', '—').
rule: An empty value shows nothing (the row is left out, or the field reads as an Add affordance once). Where a dash must stand in a table cell, it is one style: '—'.

title: Plain words a studio owner says
why: Rows and labels read like system events, statistics or rule engines ('OM-10008’s price ended … while Vivien has it', 'Creation → Assignment 26.3h median', 'Studio default · 4', 'Runs the studio').
rule: Every title, label and status is a sentence a studio owner would say out loud; no field codes, no medians, no internal names; verbs say what happens. Each rewrite is in the Words table.

title: One look for each kind of control
why: The same job is drawn several ways: views and filters as text tabs, segmented controls, outlined and bordered chips; 'create' as eleven different verbs and looks; three ways to save; two Preview bars.
rule: One house piece per job: Tabs to switch a view, the scope pill + Filters to narrow a list, one create button ('New …' + ▾) in one place, autosave (or one Save) on settings pages, one card head, one Preview bar.

title: One format for dates, money and time
why: Six to eight date styles in one module; the same amount shows as 'S$ 13,370' and 'S$13,370.04'; one meeting shows two different times.
rule: Dates: '24 Oct' this year, '24 Oct ’25' otherwise, 'today · yesterday · tomorrow' near now; money: 'S$ 13,370' on cards and tiles, 'S$13,370.04' only on documents; the house clock '2:00 PM'.

title: Never cut the fact that matters
why: Truncation hides the key fact (Company panel help lines, the deal on a Marketplace card, a task's title, Finance's 'What to know').
rule: Text that a decision rests on wraps to a second line instead of '…'; only names in a dense table may truncate, with the full words in the house tooltip.

title: Sentence case everywhere
why: Buttons, menus and column names mix Title Case and sentence case on the same menu ('Add Task' beside 'New ticket', 'Contact Log' beside 'Contact log').
rule: Sentence case for every button, menu row, column, heading and tab; proper names keep their capitals.

title: Long pages fold
why: Some pages draw everything open: a 120-row permission matrix (8,123 px), 232 message previews (26,324 px), seven report tables half of them empty, a 51-row inbox unrolled in its card, 17-row menus.
rule: A page shows the summary and the first few rows; the rest folds behind 'Show all n' or opens in a drawer; menus stay under ten rows (group or split them); an empty table is one line, not a table.

title: Phones get designed cards and a useful first screen
why: On a phone, Finance lists are tables turned sideways (seven label lines a card), chips lose their words, every card has its own ⋮ and verb line, and the first screen is the header and the AI brief.
rule: Every list on a phone uses the Leads card model (two lines + one action); chips keep their words; the first screen shows what needs doing; the Maison AI button never covers a row.

title: One home per place, named plainly
why: Tools mixes the studio's Quotes and Contracts with AI tools and has two 3D tools; 'Qanvast Ops' reads as Qanvast's console; Finance and Reports hide in Company; the rail and the phone dock order things differently.
rule: Name and place each module where a studio owner looks for it: the daily work on the rail in one order everywhere, the AI tools in Tools, the studio's Qanvast account named as such; settings live in one place (Settings vs Company split decided once).

title: Numbers and states that disagree
why: Some screens contradict each other: three counts for the same approvals, an amount that differs between a row and its pane, two different 'Profit' figures a tab apart, a portal card saying 'under way' above one saying 'paused', a contract's date 13 days off its record.
rule: One number for one fact, read from one place (the Dashboard's D5 rule applied across modules); a state is written once and shown the same everywhere.

title: Defects to fix whatever else is decided
why: Things that are simply broken: text squeezed into a few words a line at 1440, Esc taking you off the lead, a ghost that doesn’t match its page, rows that don’t line up, notification previews that all link to a lead.
rule: Fix each where it is; none needs a design call.
